title: Runoff loss after 1997 did not jump at the Victoria - New South Wales border; the 1997 step followed the winter-rain share, not the state line (CAMELS-AUS, 1951-2021)
abstract: Question: after 1997, south-east Australian runoff fell below its 1951-1996 rain relation. Earlier work found a 1997-98 step in Victoria but a gradual decline in New South Wales (NSW). Is this a state (institutional) effect or a geographic one? Climate is continuous across the Victoria-NSW border, but gauging agencies, rating practice and water and land policy are not. Approach: CAMELS-AUS v2.03 daily flow with AGCD and SILO rain; 166 Victorian and NSW/ACT catchments, 221 with Queensland and South Australia. Per catchment, Q = a + bP + cP(t-1) fitted on 1951-1996; departures, a 1951-1996 trend and a step (1997-2019 minus 1985-1996). Local-linear border jumps and band means, with a 1-degree cell bootstrap. The plan came first; the near/far, rain-season and east-wide analyses are post hoc. Results: the planned primary jump (AGCD, 2010-2019, 150 km) was +11.1 points, Victoria minus NSW (95% interval -24.1 to +29.2); by the plan this is unresolved, because only one long NSW record lies within 50 km. Band means within 150 km were equal: -21.4% against -25.9% (AGCD) and -14.3% against -12.4% (SILO). The 1997-2009 rain anomaly was -18% on both sides. The step contrast was -11.9 points (-18.9 to -5.7) more than 150 km from the border but +0.6 (-7.7 to +10.5) within 150 km. Across 221 eastern catchments the step changed with the May-October rain share, from +6.5 points (share below 0.3) to -16.6 (above 0.65); with the share in the model, state terms were not different from zero. Within Victoria the step fell by 10-13 points per 0.1 of winter-rain share (AGCD interval touches zero, SILO does not). Local 1997-2009 rain deficit did not predict the step. The pre-1997 decline was strongest in mixed-regime NSW catchments (-14% per decade) and was already visible on the NSW side of the border in 1983-1996. Conclusion: Victorian institutions did not make a larger loss at the border. The 1997 step is a property of winter-rain catchments, not of the state, and not a simple dose response to drought depth. The older NSW decline is a separate signal with an open cause. Limitations: few NSW catchments near the border; primary test unresolved; most analyses post hoc; season share and latitude are correlated; no direct gauging, rating or farm-dam data.

citations.reason: Found a Victorian 1997-98 step and a gradual NSW decline. At the state border the step contrast disappears, so the step is a geographic (rain-season) gradient, not a state effect; the early NSW decline remains.
Protected catchments lost as much runoff as farmed ones; our border test also finds no state-institution signal in the post-1997 loss.
Post-1997 loss of runoff response to rain in 175 south-east Australian catchments; same data family and annual model form.
Long-record context: multidecadal variation of runoff efficiency before 1997.
Fixed rain-gauge networks confirm the deficit; SILO drifts low after 2009, as in our SILO/AGCD ratio check.
Root-zone storage growth explains little of the loss; our result points to winter-rain catchments.
Victorian stream-side water tables and connection state.
A fixed pre-1981 rain model did not resolve the Victoria-NSW step difference; we use a border design instead.
Climate-adjusted efficiency fell in steps near 1957 and 2010; daily climate explained at most one third.
Cool-season rain loss explains part of the 2010-2025 deficit; we find the step size follows the winter-rain share across catchments.
Seven climate terms did not explain the deficit at long-record gauges.
Rain-product choice changes decline estimates; we report AGCD and SILO.
